scene: You come home in the evening and your brother greets you.
en: “Hello! Are you tired?” “Yes, I am tired. I worked for a long time.”
explain: _fessus sum_ = I am tired (a woman says _fessa sum_). _diū_ = for a long time. _labōrāvī_ is the perfect, “I worked”: the work is finished.
distractors: _labōrō_ means “I work” (now). Something finished needs the perfect: _labōrāvī_.

en: “Are you hungry?” “Yes, I am hungry and thirsty.”
explain: _esuriō_ = I am hungry, _sitiō_ = I am thirsty. Both end in _-ō_, “I”.

en: “I am preparing dinner. What do you want to eat?” “I want to eat fish and bread.”
tag: what do you want to eat?
explain: _volō_ + infinitive: _edere volō_ (I want to eat). The foods are accusative: _piscem et pānem_.
distractors: What you eat is the object: accusative _piscem_.
_nōlō_ means “I do not want”. You want to eat: _volō_.

en: “Good! Do you sleep after dinner?” “Yes, after dinner I sleep.”
explain: _post_ (after) takes the accusative: _post cēnam_. _dormiō_ is “I sleep”.

scene: A friend asks what you do each day.
en: “What are you doing today?” “Today I work in the garden.”
explain: _in hortō_ = in the garden: _in_ + ablative means “in”. _labōrō_ = I work.
distractors: _in hortum_ would mean “into the garden”. “In the garden” is _in hortō_ (ablative).
_labōrāvī_ is “I worked” (past). “Today I work” is the present: _labōrō_.

en: “And what did you do yesterday?” “Yesterday I read a book.”
explain: _lēgī_ is the perfect of _legō_: “I read” (past). _herī_ = yesterday. _librum_ is the object.
distractors: _legō_ is “I read” (now). For yesterday use the perfect: _lēgī_.
What you read is the object: accusative _librum_.

en: “And tomorrow? What will you do?” “Tomorrow I will dine with friends.”
explain: _cēnābō_ is the future of _cēnō_: “I will dine”. _cum amīcīs_ = with friends (_cum_ takes the ablative).
distractors: _cēnō_ is “I dine” (now). For tomorrow use the future: _cēnābō_.

scene: A Roman asks about your Latin.
en: “Are you learning the Latin language?” “Yes, I am learning the Latin language.”
explain: _linguam Latīnam_ is “the Latin language”: both words are accusative, and the adjective _Latīnam_ matches the noun _linguam_ (feminine).
distractors: What you learn is the object: accusative _linguam_.

en: “Is it difficult?” “It is a little difficult.”
explain: _paulum_ = a little. _difficilis est_ = it is difficult. (_difficilis_ is the form for a feminine word like _lingua_.)

en: “Do you understand me?” “Yes, a little. Say it again, please.”
la: Etiam, paulum intellegō. Dīc iterum, quaesō.
accept: Etiam, paulum intellegō. Iterum dīc, quaesō.
explain: _iterum_ = again. _dīc_ is the command “say!” to one person; _quaesō_ makes it polite.
distractors: Etiam, paulum intellegis. Dīc iterum, quaesō.
Minimē, paulum intellegō. Dīc iterum, quaesō.
_minimē_ means “no”. You do understand a little: _etiam_.
Etiam, paulum intellegō. Dīcite iterum, quaesō.
_dīcite_ is the command to several people. To one person: _dīc_.
